readerTitle: Why a raise can feel like an insult
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 주방, 소프트웨어 회사) + 실제 연구 (Adams의 공정성 이론, Card 외 2012 급여 공개 연구)
insight: 사람은 보상의 크기보다 옆 사람과의 비교로 공정함을 판단한다. 그래서 보상 결정은 비교될 것을 전제로 설계해야 한다.
misconception: 충분히 올려 주면 만족한다. 급여는 비밀로 두면 비교 문제가 생기지 않는다.

sources.text: Adams, J. S. (1963). Toward an understanding of inequity. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 67(5).
Card, D., Mas, A., Moretti, E., & Saez, E. (2012). Inequality at Work: The Effect of Peer Salaries on Job Satisfaction. American Economic Review, 102(6).
레스토랑과 소프트웨어 회사 사례, 모든 급여 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Card 외(2012) 연구 내용 확인: 2008년 Sacramento Bee가 캘리포니아 주 공무원(UC 직원 포함) 급여 검색 사이트를 공개했고, 연구진이 무작위로 일부 UC 직원에게 사이트를 알렸다. 소속 단위·직종 중위값보다 급여가 낮은 직원은 만족도가 낮아지고 이직 탐색 의향이 높아졌으며, 중위값보다 높은 직원은 뚜렷한 변화가 없었다. 카드 문장이 이 결론을 넘지 않는지, URL(DOI 10.1257/aer.102.6.2981)이 맞는지 확인 필요.
Adams 공정성 이론의 대표 출처 연도(1963 논문, 1965 확장판)를 확인하세요. 카드에는 1960년대로만 적었습니다.
가상 수치 확인: Maria 시급 $18 → $19 (+$1), 신입 시급 $20. 엔지니어 사례의 $30,000 차이는 설명용 가상 수치.

cards.title: Why a raise can feel like an insult
body: Maria has run the grill at a busy bistro for three years. On Monday she gets a raise, from $18 to $19 an hour. She's pleased.
On Friday, a new cook mentions he started at $20. Maria's pay hasn't changed since Monday. But the raise now feels like a slap.

image.label: Line cook at a grill, looking at a coworker across the kitchen
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 레스토랑 주방에서 경력 있는 요리사(여성)가 그릴 앞에 서서, 앞치마가 새것인 신입 요리사를 복잡한 표정으로 바라본다. 두 사람 머리 위에 작은 말풍선 "$19"와 "$20". 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Maria knows. Now what?
body: You own the bistro. Cooks are hard to find, so you offered the new hire $20 to get him. Maria comes to you upset.

options.text: Tell her pay is private and her raise was already generous
options.feedback: It avoids a pay bump today. But she now believes three years of loyalty count for less than one week, and she may start looking elsewhere.

options.text: Explain the hiring market honestly and raise her to at least $20
options.feedback: It costs about $1 an hour. In return you fix the comparison that hurts and show her experience is valued.

options.text: Give her a one-time $500 bonus to smooth things over
options.feedback: It shows you care, but the gap is still there on every paycheck. The feeling tends to come back.

cards.title: The money didn't change. The comparison did.
body: On Monday, Maria compared $19 with $18. On Friday, she compared herself with the new cook: more skill, more years, less pay.
Nothing about her own deal got worse. What changed was the person she measured it against. That shift turned a reward into a grievance.

cards.title: Fairness is a comparison
body: In the 1960s, psychologist J. Stacy Adams described what he called equity. People weigh what they **give** (effort, skill, years) against what they **get** (pay, perks, credit). Then they compare that balance with people around them.
If the balance looks worse than a peer's, people feel cheated. They may cut effort, complain or leave. The absolute amount matters less than the gap.

image.label: Two balance scales side by side, one tipped unfairly
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 저울 두 개를 나란히 배치. 왼쪽 저울 "Maria": 한쪽에 "3 years, skill" 무거운 추, 다른 쪽 "$19". 오른쪽 저울 "New cook": "1 week" 가벼운 추와 "$20". 두 저울 사이에 "compare" 화살표.

cards.title: What happened when salaries went public
body: In 2008, a California newspaper put state employee salaries online, including University of California staff. Economists David Card and colleagues then told a random group of university employees about the site.

Those who learned they earned **below the middle** for their job and unit became less satisfied and more likely to say they were job hunting. Those above the middle showed little change. Losing a comparison hurt far more than winning one helped.

cards.title: People compare everything, and judge the rules too.
body: The same test runs on tips, weekend shifts, the best tables, promotions and public praise. Who got the Saturday off is a fairness question.
People also judge **how** a decision was made. Differences are easier to accept when the rule is clear, applied the same way to everyone, and explained before anyone finds out on their own.

image.label: Staff schedule board with shifts being compared
image.brief: 주간 근무표 화이트보드 일러스트. 토요일 칸에 이름 스티커가 몰려 있고, 직원 두 명이 표를 가리키며 이야기하는 모습. 옆에 작은 메모 "How were shifts decided?". 로고 없음.

cards.title: Equal isn't the same as fair.
body: Paying everyone the same avoids awkward talks, but your strongest people may feel their extra effort is ignored, and leave.

Secrecy doesn't work either. Pay, perks and favors tend to come out eventually. A better test: make each decision as if it will be posted on the wall, with a reason you would be comfortable defending.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You run a 15-person software startup. To land a senior engineer, you need to offer $30,000 more than two current engineers with similar skills earn.

options.text: Make the offer and keep salaries confidential
options.feedback: You get the hire fast. But in a small team the gap will likely surface, and two good engineers may feel they've been underpaid all along.

options.text: Make the offer, then review the current engineers against the same market data and adjust or explain
options.feedback: It costs more now. But one clear rule applies to everyone, so the gap has a reason you can defend.

options.text: Cap the offer at current pay and lose the candidate
options.feedback: You protect internal fairness, but the team stays short-handed. Fairness is a reason to fix the system, not to stop hiring.

cards.title: People judge rewards by comparison, not by amount.
body: Before any raise, bonus or perk, ask who this person will compare it with, and whether the reason would hold up if everyone knew.
**Try it today:** pick one recent pay or shift decision. Write the one-sentence rule behind it. If you can't, that's where unfairness may be hiding.
